caption:
Baby shower's over and 20 thank-you notes left to write? Paste who gave what into AI and ask for a short note for each one.

WHY IT WORKS: the hard part of 20 notes isn't the writing, it's starting each one. Once AI knows the gift, it can say how you'll use it, and that's the line that makes a note feel personal. Asking for them to sound different stops 20 copies of the same sentence.

THE REAL TEST: we made up a baby shower with 20 guests and gifts and asked Claude (Anthropic) on Nov 3, 2026: "My baby shower was on Saturday and I have 20 thank-you notes to write today. Here's who gave what: [1. Aunt Rosa: a handmade quilt … 20. My book club: a basket of snacks for late nights] Write a 2-sentence note for each one. Name the gift and say one specific way we'll use it. Don't make them all sound the same."
It wrote all 20. Note 3 (Grandpa Joe, a rocking chair he fixed up), word for word: "I can't believe how beautiful the rocking chair turned out after all your work on it. It's going right next to the crib, and every 3 a.m. feeding will happen in it."

HOW (about 15 minutes):
1. Open ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini.
2. Type each person and their gift, one per line.
3. Ask: "Write a 2-sentence note for each one. Name the gift and say one specific way we'll use it. Don't make them all sound the same."
4. Read each note, change anything that isn't true for you, then copy it into the card by hand.

THE CATCH: AI guesses details it can't know: read every note and fix anything that isn't true before you send. It wrote about a nursery chair, morning walks and the spot next to the crib, and for the $50 gift card it wrote "We're going to use it to stock up on diapers and wipes". None of that came from us. Add one real detail of your own where you can.

PRIVACY TIP: first names and the gift are enough. Leave out addresses, last names and anything about anyone's health.

Names and gifts made up for this post.

Do this: Paste names and gifts. Ask for notes. Edit before you send.

Send this to whoever has a stack of cards to write.

Follow to learn one real AI trick a day.

caption:
Store closes at 9 and no plan for the week? Ask AI for 5 dinners that share ingredients, with one shopping list.

WHY IT WORKS: food goes to waste when each recipe needs its own half-bag of something. Asking for dinners that share ingredients makes AI plan the week as one shop: the same chicken, peppers and beans turn up on different nights, so the list gets shorter and less is left over.

THE REAL TEST: we made up the ask and gave it to Claude (Anthropic) on Nov 3, 2026: "The grocery store closes at 9 and I need to shop for the week. Plan 5 weeknight dinners for 2 adults, each under 30 minutes, that share ingredients so nothing goes to waste. Budget about $80. Give me the 5 dinners (one line each), then one shopping list, then tell me which ingredients get used more than once. Keep it short."
Its 5 dinners, word for word: "Mon: Chicken fajitas." · "Tue: Chicken fried rice." · "Wed: Black bean quesadillas." · "Thu: Garlic chicken and broccoli pasta." · "Fri: Rice and bean burrito bowls."
It priced the list at "about $70 to $80" (its estimate), and listed what gets reused, word for word: "Chicken: Mon, Tue, Thu" · "Bell peppers: Mon, Wed, Fri" · "Black beans: Wed, Fri".

HOW (5 minutes before you leave):
1. Open ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini.
2. Say how many dinners, for how many people, how much time and your budget.
3. Ask for dinners "that share ingredients so nothing goes to waste", one shopping list, and which ingredients get used more than once.
4. Cross off what you already have, then shop the list.

THE CATCH: read the plan before you trust it. One of its tips said "Rice: Tue, Fri. Cook a double batch Tuesday, since day-old rice is better for fried rice anyway." But the fried rice is on Tuesday, so to have day-old rice, cook it Monday night. Prices are its guesses, not your store's.

PRIVACY TIP: "2 adults, about $80" is all it needs. No names, address or health details.

caption:
16°C inside and the landlord still hasn't fixed the heat? Tell AI what's wrong, since when, what you've done and what you need, and ask for a short, polite but firm email.

AI, for real · Day 13. One real test of what AI can do, with the output shown.

WHY IT WORKS: when you're cold and annoyed, the email comes out either too soft or too angry. Giving AI the four facts (what's wrong, since when, what you've already done, what you need by when) gets you a message that's calm, dated and hard to ignore, and a written record if you need one later.

THE REAL TEST (names, unit and dates made up for this post), Claude (Anthropic):
Prompt: "Today is Friday, November 6. The heat in my apartment has been off since Wednesday, November 4, and it's 16°C inside. I texted my landlord, Dan, on Wednesday and he said he'd look at it, but nothing has happened. Write me a short email to send him before 5 pm today. Polite but firm: what's wrong, since when, what I've already done, and that I need the heat repaired by Saturday, November 7. Sign it from Alex in unit 4B. Under 120 words."
Slide 2 is its email, word for word. Notice it turned our ask into one clear request with a time: "Please let me know today when someone will come, and I'll make sure they can get in."

THE CATCH: AI doesn't know the rules where you live. Heat and repair rules for rentals depend on your province or city, so check your local tenant rules before you quote any of them. Keep a copy of the email and of your first text, and check every date in the draft before you send it.

PRIVACY TIP: you don't need to paste your lease, your landlord's details or your phone number. A first name and unit number are enough to draft it.

Do this: in ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini, type what's wrong, since when, what you've already done, and what you need by when. Then ask: "Write me a short email. Polite but firm. Under 120 words."

Send this to whoever's waiting on a repair.
